```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)

snapshot <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/main/Week10B/data/"

accent   <- "#2a78d6"
accent_2 <- "#eb6834"
theme_nb <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")
```

# The API

The Nobel Prize Developer Zone publishes a public API that needs no key. I used the **laureates**
endpoint, `https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates`, which returns one record per laureate with
every prize that laureate has won nested inside it.

```{r}
#| label: live-call
resp <- request("https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates") |>
  req_url_query(limit = 1) |>
  req_error(is_error = \(r) FALSE) |>
  req_perform()

parsed <- resp_body_json(resp)

tibble(
  status            = resp_status(resp),
  laureates_in_api  = parsed$meta$count,
  returned_this_call = length(parsed$laureates)
)
```

## What one record looks like

A laureate is not a row. It is a deeply nested object: names repeat in up to three languages, birth
sits inside its own object with a place inside that, and prizes arrive as an array because some
laureates have won more than once.

```{r}
#| label: structure
one <- parsed$laureates[[1]]

tibble(
  field = c("knownName", "birth", "birth$place$country", "nobelPrizes", "affiliations"),
  shape = c(
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$knownName), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$birth), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$birth$place$country), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("array of", length(one$nobelPrizes), "prize object(s)"),
    paste("array inside each prize, with name / city / country objects")
  )
)
```

Three further wrinkles shape every decision below: **organizations** such as the Red Cross appear
alongside people but carry `orgName` and `founded` instead of `knownName` and `birth`, with no
gender; **results are paginated**, 100 at a time; and some birth dates record only a year, written
as `1948-00-00`.

# Retrieving and Tidying the Data

The collection script pages through the whole list, flattens each record, and writes two tidy
tables. The key part is the flattening:

```{r}
#| label: flatten-code
#| eval: false
# English label from a multi-language field, e.g. {en: "USA", se: "USA"}
en <- function(x) if (is.null(x)) NA_character_ else (x[["en"]] %||% NA_character_)

# First non-missing value. en() returns NA (not NULL) for an absent field and
# %||% only catches NULL, so organizations need a fallback that treats NA as
# "try the next one" — otherwise every organization loses its name.
first_present <- function(...) {
  vals <- c(...)
  vals <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
  if (length(vals)) vals[[1]] else NA_character_
}

laureates <- map_dfr(laureates_raw, \(l) tibble(
  laureate_id     = l$id,
  name            = first_present(en(l$knownName), en(l$orgName)),
  is_organization = !is.null(l$orgName),
  gender          = l$gender %||% NA_character_,
  birth_date      = first_present(l$birth$date %||% NA_character_,
                                  l$founded$date %||% NA_character_),
  birth_country_now = first_present(en(l$birth$place$countryNow),
                                    en(l$founded$place$countryNow)),
  n_prizes        = length(l$nobelPrizes)
))

# One row per laureate per prize: a two-time winner becomes two rows.
prizes <- map_dfr(laureates_raw, \(l) {
  map_dfr(l$nobelPrizes, \(p) {
    aff <- if (length(p$affiliations)) p$affiliations[[1]] else NULL
    tibble(
      laureate_id             = l$id,
      award_year              = as.integer(p$awardYear),
      category                = en(p$category),
      prize_status            = p$prizeStatus %||% NA_character_,
      affiliation_country_now = if (is.null(aff)) NA_character_ else en(aff$countryNow)
    )
  })
})
```

The full script is
[`fetch_nobel.R`](https://github.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/blob/main/Week10B/fetch_nobel.R). Its
output is saved to CSV so this report renders from a fixed snapshot rather than a live call.

```{r}
#| label: load
laureates <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nobel_laureates.csv"),
                      col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  mutate(is_organization = as.logical(is_organization),
         n_prizes        = as.integer(n_prizes),
         # Year only: 48 birth dates are recorded as e.g. 1948-00-00, so the
         # year is reliable but the exact date is not.
         birth_year      = as.integer(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4)))

prizes <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nobel_prizes.csv"),
                   col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  mutate(award_year = as.integer(award_year))

# One row per laureate-prize, with the laureate's own details attached.
awards <- prizes |>
  left_join(
    laureates |> select(laureate_id, is_organization, gender, birth_year,
                        birth_country, birth_country_now),
    by = "laureate_id"
  )

tibble(
  laureate_records   = nrow(laureates),
  laureate_prize_rows = nrow(awards),
  repeat_winners     = sum(laureates$n_prizes > 1),
  organizations      = sum(laureates$is_organization),
  years_covered      = paste(min(awards$award_year), "-", max(awards$award_year))
)
```

Seven laureates have won more than once, producing the eight extra prize rows:

```{r}
#| label: repeats
laureates |>
  filter(n_prizes > 1) |>
  select(name, is_organization, n_prizes) |>
  arrange(desc(n_prizes))
```

## Cleaning decisions

```{r}
#| label: missing
bind_rows(
  laureates |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
    mutate(table = "laureates"),
  prizes |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
    mutate(table = "prizes")
) |>
  filter(missing > 0) |>
  select(table, column, missing)
```

Each gap is kept rather than patched, with a reason:

- **`gender` is missing for all `r sum(laureates$is_organization)` organizations.** They are
  excluded from the gender question rather than counted as unknown.
- **`affiliation_country` is missing for `r sum(is.na(prizes$affiliation_country_now))` prizes.**
  Peace and Literature laureates usually have no institutional affiliation. These are excluded from
  Question 4, which needs both countries, and the report states how many rows that leaves.
- **`death_date` is missing for `r sum(is.na(laureates$death_date))` laureates**, who are living.
  That is information, not absence.
- **Country names are taken from `countryNow`** rather than `country`. The raw field records the
  country as it was named at the time, so Marie Curie's birthplace is "Russian Empire" while
  `countryNow` says "Poland". Using present-day names makes countries comparable across 125 years.

```{r}
#| label: status
prizes |> count(prize_status)
```

Two prizes were declined and one is restricted. They stay in the counts, because the prize was
still awarded.

# Question 1: How has the number of laureates changed over time?

**The question.** The prize has grown from a handful of awards a year to a crowded field. Counting
by decade and category shows when that happened.

```{r}
#| label: q1-table
by_decade <- awards |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  count(decade, category)

by_decade |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(laureates = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Decade", "Laureates"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1
#| fig-cap: "Laureates per decade by category. The 2020s are incomplete, covering 2020 to 2026."
#| fig-height: 3.8
by_decade |>
  mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, n, sum, .desc = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Laureates per decade, by category",
       x = NULL, y = "Laureates") +
  theme_nb +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

**The answer.** Numbers roughly doubled: the 1900s produced 57 laureates and the 2000s produced 123.
The cause is sharing rather than more prizes — a single prize is now routinely split between two or
three people, where early prizes usually went to one. Economic Sciences only begins in 1969, which
is visible as the category appearing part-way along.

# Question 2: How has the share of women changed?

**The question.** Women are a small minority of laureates. Is that changing, and does it differ by
category?

```{r}
#| label: q2-people
people <- awards |> filter(!is_organization)

people |>
  count(gender) |>
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Gender", "Prizes", "%"))
```

```{r}
#| label: q2-category
people |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    prizes      = n(),
    women       = sum(gender == "female"),
    pct_women   = round(100 * sum(gender == "female") / n(), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_women)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Prizes", "Women", "% women"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2
#| fig-cap: "Share of prizes to women by decade. Organizations are excluded, since they have no gender."
#| fig-height: 3.4
people |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(pct_women = 100 * sum(gender == "female") / n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = pct_women)) +
  geom_col(fill = accent, width = 8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct_women)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "The share of women has risen, from a very low base",
       x = NULL, y = "% of prizes to women") +
  theme_nb
```

**The answer.** The share has risen from 5.4% in the 1900s to 19.5% in the 2020s, with the 1950s
recording none at all. The gap between categories is wider than the change over time: Peace sits at
18.6% and Literature at 15.4%, while Physics is at 2.2% — five women in 231 prizes.

# Question 3: How old are laureates when they win?

**The question.** The prize is often awarded long after the work it recognises. Age at the time of
the award makes that lag visible, and shows whether it is growing.

```{r}
#| label: q3-age
ages <- people |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_year)) |>
  mutate(age = award_year - birth_year)

tibble(
  prizes_with_age = nrow(ages),
  mean_age        = round(mean(ages$age), 1),
  median_age      = median(ages$age),
  youngest        = min(ages$age),
  oldest          = max(ages$age)
)
```

Age here is **award year minus birth year**, not an exact age in years. That is a deliberate
simplification: 48 birth dates record only a year, so a precise calculation would silently drop
them. The approximation is at most a year out.

```{r}
#| label: q3-category
ages |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(prizes = n(), mean_age = round(mean(age), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(mean_age) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Prizes", "Mean age"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q3
#| fig-cap: "Age at the time of the award. Each point is one prize; the line is a smoothed trend."
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(ages, aes(x = award_year, y = age)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.4, color = accent) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = accent_2, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Laureates are winning later in life",
       x = "Award year", y = "Age at award") +
  theme_nb
```

```{r}
#| label: q3-extremes
bind_rows(
  ages |> slice_min(age, n = 3) |> mutate(group = "Youngest"),
  ages |> slice_max(age, n = 3) |> mutate(group = "Oldest")
) |>
  select(group, name, category, award_year, age) |>
  kable(col.names = c("", "Name", "Category", "Year", "Age"))
```

**The answer.** The mean is 60.6 and the median 61, but the trend is the real finding: laureates
awarded before 1970 averaged 55.2, and those since average 64.0 — nearly nine years older.
Economic Sciences has the oldest laureates at 67.2 and Physics the youngest at 57.8. The range runs
from Malala Yousafzai at 17 to John B. Goodenough at 97.

# Question 4: Which countries lost laureates, and which gained them?

**The question.** This one needs two fields compared rather than counted. Each prize record holds
the laureate's **country of birth** and the **country of the institution they were working at** when
they won. Where those differ, a country educated someone whose prize was credited elsewhere.

```{r}
#| label: q4-prepare
movers <- awards |>
  filter(
    !is_organization,                      # organizations have no birthplace
    !is.na(birth_country_now),             # both countries must be known
    !is.na(affiliation_country_now)
  ) |>
  mutate(moved = birth_country_now != affiliation_country_now)

tibble(
  all_prize_rows      = nrow(awards),
  organizations       = sum(awards$is_organization),
  no_affiliation      = sum(is.na(awards$affiliation_country_now)),
  usable_for_question = nrow(movers),
  moved               = sum(movers$moved),
  pct_moved           = round(100 * mean(movers$moved), 1)
)
```

Only `r nrow(movers)` of `r nrow(awards)` prize rows can answer this, because Peace and Literature
laureates usually have no listed institution. The result describes the laureates who worked at
universities and laboratories, which is most of the science prizes.

```{r}
#| label: q4-net
lost   <- movers |> filter(moved) |> count(country = birth_country_now,       name = "lost")
gained <- movers |> filter(moved) |> count(country = affiliation_country_now, name = "gained")

net_flow <- full_join(lost, gained, by = "country") |>
  replace_na(list(lost = 0, gained = 0)) |>
  mutate(net = gained - lost)

bind_rows(
  net_flow |> slice_max(net, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Biggest net gainers"),
  net_flow |> slice_min(net, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Biggest net losers")
) |>
  select(group, country, lost, gained, net) |>
  kable(col.names = c("", "Country", "Laureates lost", "Laureates gained", "Net"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q4
#| fig-cap: "Net movement of laureates: born in one country, awarded while working in another."
#| fig-height: 4
net_flow |>
  filter(abs(net) >= 4) |>
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, net),
         direction = if_else(net > 0, "Net gain", "Net loss")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = net, y = country, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = net), hjust = ifelse(net_flow |> filter(abs(net) >= 4) |> pull(net) > 0, -0.3, 1.3),
            size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Net gain" = accent, "Net loss" = accent_2), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  labs(title = "One country gains; everyone else loses",
       x = "Laureates gained minus laureates lost", y = NULL) +
  theme_nb +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: q4-flows
movers |>
  filter(moved) |>
  count(birth_country_now, affiliation_country_now, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Born in", "Awarded while working in", "Laureates"))
```

```{r}
#| label: q4-us
movers |>
  summarise(
    born_in_usa      = sum(birth_country_now == "USA"),
    affiliated_usa   = sum(affiliation_country_now == "USA"),
    prizes           = n()
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_born = round(100 * born_in_usa / prizes, 1),
         pct_affiliated = round(100 * affiliated_usa / prizes, 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Born in USA", "Working in USA", "Prizes", "% born", "% working"))
```

**The answer.** Just under a third of these prizes, `r round(100 * mean(movers$moved), 1)`%, went to
someone working outside their country of birth, and the flow is overwhelmingly in one direction.
**The United States has a net gain of 130 laureates**, losing only 4 while gaining 134. No other
country comes close: the United Kingdom is next at +11, and Switzerland at +9.

The largest losers are Poland (−19), then Canada, Scotland, Austria, Hungary, Russia and the
Netherlands. The single biggest flow is United Kingdom to USA, 19 laureates, followed by Canada to
USA at 15 and Germany to USA at 11.

The clearest way to see it: **35.7% of these laureates were born in the United States, but 52.8%
were working there when they won.**

```{r}
#| label: q4-era
movers |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(prizes = n(), n_moved = sum(moved),
            pct_moved = round(100 * sum(moved) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Decade", "Prizes", "Moved", "% moved"))
```

Interestingly, the share who moved has **not** risen much: it was 42% in the 1900s and 36% in the
2020s, hovering around a third throughout. What changed is the destination. The early movements were
largely within Europe — Poland to Germany is the fourth-largest flow in the whole dataset — while
the modern ones nearly all end in the United States.

# Conclusions

- **The prize has roughly doubled in size**, from 57 laureates in the 1900s to 123 in the 2000s,
  mostly because prizes are now shared between two or three people.
- **Women have gone from 5.4% of laureates to 19.5%**, but the category gap is larger than the
  change over time: Peace is at 18.6% and Physics at 2.2%.
- **Laureates are winning almost nine years later in life** than before 1970, 64.0 against 55.2,
  which suggests a lengthening gap between the work and its recognition.
- **The United States has gained 130 laureates it did not produce**, while Poland has lost 19. A
  third of scientific laureates were working outside their country of birth when they won, and that
  share has been roughly constant for a century — only the destination has changed.

**What the data cannot say.** Question 4 rests on 761 of 1,036 prize rows, because Peace and
Literature laureates rarely list an institution, so it is really a finding about the sciences. The
affiliation is also only the one recorded at the time of the award: a laureate who was born in
Germany, trained in the UK and won in the USA appears here simply as Germany to USA.

# Source

Nobel Prize API v2.1, laureates endpoint, <https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates>. Data from
nobelprize.org, used under the
[Nobel Prize API terms of use](https://www.nobelprize.org/about/terms-of-use-for-api-nobelprize-org-and-data-nobelprize-org/).
